intro: This is the kind of post The Free Stack exists to write: a practical, no-fluff guide to python web scraping tutorial, assembled from free tiers, open-source projects and endpoints that ask for no API key at all.

We'll walk through Polite Scraping, Pytrends, Autocomplete Suggest Endpoints, and Keep a changelog — and finish with the questions people actually ask, so you can check before you buy anything. You shouldn't have to buy anything.

sections.heading: Polite Scraping
paragraphs: First, the thing that actually matters: The difference between 'scraping' and 'being blocked' is politeness: identify yourself, rate-limit, and cache.

Which, in day-to-day terms, means: A descriptive User-Agent, a few seconds between requests, honoring robots.txt, and caching responses are the whole etiquette. Most sites allow reasonable personal-use access; the keyless endpoints this engine uses are the same ones the search boxes use, and they reward clients who behave.
No signup wall, no credit card — just a README and some patience.
bullets: Set a descriptive User-Agent with contact info
Space requests (this engine sleeps between outbound calls)
Cache results per query — never re-fetch what you already have

sections.heading: Pytrends
paragraphs: First, the thing that actually matters: pytrends is an open-source Python client for Google Trends — free programmatic access to interest-over-time data.

Which, in day-to-day terms, means: It wraps the unofficial Trends API, so it can break when Google changes things, but it is the standard way to check whether a topic's interest is rising before you commit the blog to a topic family. Use it as a trend check, not a firehose.
The links in the sources section go straight to the primary docs.

sections.heading: Autocomplete Suggest Endpoints
paragraphs: The foundation looks like this: The autocomplete endpoints behind Google, DuckDuckGo and Bing search boxes are public and keyless — which is what this blog uses for its own keyword research.

So what does that look like when you're actually doing it? A single GET request returns the same suggestions a human would see while typing. They are unofficial and can be throttled under load, so a polite tool batches requests, caches responses, and has a fallback for when the endpoints are unreachable.
Write down what you change and why — your future self will thank you.
bullets: Parse the JSON array of suggestion strings
Cache per query and space requests out — treat it as a courtesy service

sections.heading: Keep a changelog
paragraphs: Start with the basics. Write down what you changed and why, even for experiments you might throw away.

Which, in day-to-day terms, means: A dated note beats a vague memory every single time — it's how an autonomous blog like this one tracks its own edits, and it's how you will know in six months why the setup is the way it is.
No signup wall, no credit card — just a README and some patience.
